# Claim handoff across nodes

Several nodes need to work on one acquisition — one stages the data, the next writes it, the last checks it — and the acquisition should resolve exactly once, at the end, on the outcome of the whole group. Rimsky spells this as **co-holdership**: one node acquires the claim, and every other node declares `holds:` against it.

The alternative is worse in a way that is easy to miss. Three nodes each declaring their own `claim_producers:` entry on the same selector make three acquisitions and three resolutions, and the producer sees three Opens.

## The shape

- One node acquires the claim and gives it an `alias`.
- Downstream nodes name that alias under `holds:` with `from:` naming the acquirer.
- Every holder reads the live claim through `{{claim.<alias>.address}}`, `{{claim.<alias>.claim_scope}}`, and `{{claim.<alias>.payload[.<field>]}}`.
- The producer sees one Open. When the holding sub-graph completes successfully it sees one Commit; when any holder fails it sees one Abandon.

## The template

```yaml
name: staged-write
version: "1"
description: One staging claim, opened once, held by a writer and a verifier, resolved once at the end.
params_schema:
  type: object
  properties:
    run:
      type: string
  required: [run]
nodes:
  - type: acquirer
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: stage-store
        selector: "/stage/{{params.run}}"
        intent: rw
        alias: staged
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable":
        action: give_up
      "acquire/producer_error":
        action: give_up
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:
            type: string
            default: "https://stage.example.internal/prepare"
          method:
            type: string
            default: POST
          held_addr:
            type: string
            source: "{{claim.staged.address}}"

  - type: writer
    executor: http-node
    holds:
      staged:
        from: acquirer
    subscribes:
      - node: acquirer
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    error_types:
      "http/server_error/500":
        action: give_up
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:
            type: string
            default: "https://stage.example.internal/write"
          method:
            type: string
            default: POST
          held_addr:
            type: string
            source: "{{claim.staged.address}}"
          held_scope:
            type: string
            source: "{{claim.staged.claim_scope}}"
          held_region:
            type: string
            source: "{{claim.staged.payload.region}}"

  - type: verifier
    executor: http-node
    holds:
      staged:
        from: acquirer
    subscribes:
      - node: writer
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    error_types:
      "http/server_error/500":
        action: give_up
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:
            type: string
            default: "https://stage.example.internal/verify"
          method:
            type: string
            default: POST
          held_addr:
            type: string
            source: "{{claim.staged.address}}"
```

## What you will see

On a clean run all three nodes settle fresh, and the producer's log for that selector reads **Open, Commit** — one Open for the whole holding sub-graph, one Commit, no Abandon. The writer and the verifier each receive the acquirer's own address byte for byte, along with the payload field and the scope bytes, so no node re-acquires. The claim handle ends `committed`, and `GET /v1/claim-handles/{id}/holders` reports three holders on that one claim.

When the verifier fails, the producer's log reads **Open, Abandon**. The claim was still opened exactly once, and the acquirer, the writer and the verifier all settle failed with `terminal/error/abandoned`. The claim handle ends `abandoned`.

That is the point of the shape: the group's outcome is the claim's outcome, and no partial write survives a downstream failure.

## Reading a co-held claim

Four directives resolve against a held alias, and they resolve identically for the acquirer and for every holder:

| Directive | Resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `{{claim.<alias>.address}}` | Where the claimed thing lives, in the producer's vocabulary |
| `{{claim.<alias>.claim_scope}}` | The opaque scope bytes the producer returned |
| `{{claim.<alias>.payload}}` | The producer's whole payload object |
| `{{claim.<alias>.payload.<field>}}` | One field of it |

`address` and `claim_scope` take no further path.

## Renaming on the way in

Two acquirers whose claims share an alias collide inside one holder. Rename with `as:`:

```yaml
    holds:
      staged:
        from: acquirer-a
        as: source
      staged-b:
        from: acquirer-b
        as: sink
```

## Making the claim outlive the sub-graph

Add `lifetime: durable` to the acquirer's claim entry. A durable claim commits the same way, but the retention sweep leaves its row alone, so later runs can co-hold it and the asset queries can find it. Releasing it takes an explicit operator action — `rimsky asset delete`, or the delete route — which calls the producer's Release verb.

## Sharp edges

**The acquirer must actually declare the alias.** `holds:` names a claim alias belonging to another node's `claim_producers:` block. A `from:` naming a node that does not declare that alias fails at registration.

**A node may not hold from itself, and the holds graph must be acyclic.** Both are registration errors.

**Failure cascades to every holder.** One holder's failure abandons the claim, and every holder — including the acquirer, which had already settled — ends at `terminal/error/abandoned`. Subscribe to `terminal/error/abandoned` if a downstream node needs to know the group came apart.

**Not every producer presents a durable claim as an asset.** The asset surface needs a producer that advertises the data-processing protocol. The bundled filesystem producer does not, so a durable claim against it persists past its sub-graph and is simply never asset-presentable. Use a producer that advertises `data_processing` when you need the asset verbs.

**The claim is held, not locked against the world.** Co-holdership coordinates the nodes of one holding sub-graph. Mutual exclusion against other instances is a different primitive — declare `locks:` on the node and a `named_locks.<name>.limit` in the deployment configuration.
